claim: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of 674 differentially expressed genes upon knockdown of YAP/TAZ (fold change > 2, p<0.05) revealed that genes downregulated by YAP/TAZ knockdown were enriched in the term P-body in the cellular component category.
source: Gene Ontology enrichment analysis of the 674 differentially expressed genes upon knockdown of YAP/TAZ (fold change [FC] > 2, p<0.05) revealed that the genes downregulated by YAP/TAZ knockdown were enriched in the term P-body in the cellular component category (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data (GSE176475) and Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: TEAD4 binds to the promoter regions of AJUBA, WTIP, NOCT, SAMD4A, and PNRC1 and to the intronic region of PNRC1 in HCT116 cells.
source: The ChIP–qPCR results in HCT116 cells further confirmed that TEAD4 bound to the promoter regions of AJUBA, WTIP, NOCT, SAMD4A, and PNRC1 and to the intronic region of PNRC1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Knockdown of YAP/TAZ significantly downregulated mRNA expression of AJUBA, WTIP, SAMD4A, and NOCT and moderately increased expression of PNRC1 in HCT116, A549, and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Next, we confirmed the significantly downregulated mRNA expression of AJUBA, WTIP, SAMD4A, and NOCT and moderately increased expression of PNRC1 in YAP/TAZ knockdown HCT116 cells by qPCR analysis; this pattern was also observed in A549 lung cancer cells and MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active YAP5SA mutant but not the TEAD binding-defective YAP5SA-S94A mutant significantly decreased the mRNA level of PNRC1 and increased the mRNA level of SAMD4A in HCT116, MCF7 and A549 cells.
source: Consistent with these findings, overexpression of the constitutively active YAP5SA mutant but not the TEAD binding-defective YAP5SA-S94A mutant significantly decreased the mRNA level of PNRC1 and increased the mRNA level of SAMD4A in HCT116, MCF7 and A549 cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Overexpression of YAP5SA but not YAP5SA-S94A decreased the protein level of PNRC1 in HCT116, A549, and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Additionally, overexpression of YAP5SA but not YAP5SA-S94A decreased the protein level of PNRC1 in HCT116, A549, and MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: YAP/TAZ modulates the transcription of P-body-related genes through the TEAD transcription factors.
source: Overall, these data demonstrate that YAP/TAZ modulates the transcription of P-body-related genes through the TEAD transcription factors.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing TEAD4 binding and differential gene expression dependent on YAP-TEAD interaction.

claim: Knockdown of YAP/TAZ significantly decreased the number of DDX6/DCP1A-positive foci in HCT116 cells.
source: We found that knockdown of YAP/TAZ significantly decreased but overexpression of YAP5SA increased the number of DDX6/DCP1A-positive foci in HCT116 cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Overexpression of YAP5SA increased the number of DDX6/DCP1A-positive foci in HCT116 cells.
source: We found that knockdown of YAP/TAZ significantly decreased but overexpression of YAP5SA increased the number of DDX6/DCP1A-positive foci in HCT116 cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HCT116 cells expressing YAP5SA-S94A and control HCT116 cells showed similar numbers of P-bodies, indicating that TEAD transcription factors mediate the enhanced effects of YAP/TAZ on P-body formation.
source: HCT116 cells expressing YAP5SA-S94A and control HCT116 cells showed similar numbers of P-bodies, which indicated that the TEAD transcription factors mediate the enhanced effects of YAP/TAZ on P-body formation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and inference from the lack of effect of the TEAD-binding defective mutant.

claim: Serum stimulation led to rapid induction of P-body formation in HCT116 and NIH3T3 cells.
source: We observed that serum stimulation led to rapid induction of P-body formation in HCT116 and NIH3T3 cells (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Knockdown of YAP/TAZ attenuated the enhancement of P-body formation induced by serum stimulation.
source: Knockdown of YAP/TAZ attenuated the enhancement of P-body formation induced by serum stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: At high cell density, the number of P-bodies was significantly decreased in HCT116 and NIH3T3 cells.
source: Conversely, at a high cell density, the number of P-bodies was significantly decreased in HCT116 and NIH3T3 cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The expression of SAMD4A, NOCT, and WTIP in HCT116 cells was induced by serum stimulation and suppressed by culture at high cell density.
source: Consistent with this finding, the expression of SAMD4A, NOCT, and WTIP in HCT116 cells was induced by serum stimulation and suppressed by culture at a high cell density (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Both serum starvation and culture at high cell density dramatically increased the expression of PNRC1.
source: Intriguingly, both serum starvation and culture at a high cell density dramatically increased the expression of PNRC1, consistent with the tumor suppressor function of PNRC1 (Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and G, and inference about tumor suppressor function.

claim: When NIH3T3 cells were shifted from soft (1 kPa) to stiff (40 kPa) matrices, YAP was translocated into nucleus and activated.
source: When NIH3T3 cells were shifted from soft (1 kPa) to stiff (40 kPa) matrices, YAP was translocated into nucleus and activated (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: P-body formation was enhanced when NIH3T3 cells were cultured on stiff matrices compared to soft matrices, which was associated with decreased mRNA level of Pnrc1 and increased mRNA levels of Ajuba, Samd4, and Noct.
source: Furthermore, the P-body formation was enhanced, which was associated with decreased mRNA level of Pnrc1 and increased mRNA levels of Ajuba, Samd4, and Noct (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and H.

claim: YAP/TAZ are positive regulators of P-body formation in response to various stimuli, probably by modulating the expression of P-body-related genes.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that YAP/TAZ could be positive regulators of P-body formation in response to various stimuli, probably by modulating the expression of P-body-related genes.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing YAP/TAZ effects on P-body formation under different conditions and gene expression changes.

claim: Knockdown of both AJUBA and SAMD4A significantly diminished the promoting effect of YAP5SA overexpression on P-body formation in HCT116 cells.
source: As expected, knockdown of both AJUBA and SAMD4A significantly diminished the promoting effect of YAP5SA overexpression on P-body formation in HCT116 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PNRC1 is a tumor suppressor that inhibits P-body formation by recruiting cytoplasmic DCP1A/DCP2 into the nucleolus.
source: Unlike AJUBA and SAMD4A, PNRC1 is a tumor suppressor that inhibits P-body formation by recruiting cytoplasmic DCP1A/DCP2 into the nucleolus, thus loss of cytoplasmic DCP1A/DCP2 results in disruption of P-body (Gaviraghi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaviraghi et al., 2018.

claim: Overexpression of WT PNRC1 but not the W300A mutant dramatically decreased the number of P-bodies in YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 cells.
source: We observed that overexpression of WT PNRC1 but not the W300A mutant dramatically decreased the number of P-bodies in YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The reduction in P-body number was reversed by knockdown of PNRC1 in YAP/TAZ knockdown HCT116 cells.
source: Consistent with the above findings, the reduction in the P-body number was reversed by knockdown of PNRC1 in YAP/TAZ knockdown HCT116 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: YAP/TAZ enhances P-body formation through modulation of a series of P-body-related genes, with both activation of SAMD4A and AJUBA expression and downregulation of PNRC1 involved.
source: Collectively, these findings indicate that YAP/TAZ enhances P-body formation through modulation of a series of P-body-related genes. Both activation of SAMD4A and AJUBA expression and downregulation of PNRC1 are involved in YAP/TAZ-induced P-body formation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing effects of knockdown/overexpression of these genes on P-body formation.

claim: Overexpression of YAP5SA significantly decreased the luciferase activity of both the PNRC1 promoter and intron reporters.
source: We observed that overexpression of YAP5SA significantly decreased the luciferase activity of both the PNRC1 promoter and intron reporters (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The S94A mutation in YAP resulted in a decreased suppressive effect on PNRC1 promoter and intron luciferase reporter activity compared to the 5SA mutation.
source: Compared with the 5SA mutation in YAP, the S94A mutation resulted in a decreased suppressive effect on PNRC1 promoter and intron luciferase reporter activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The luciferase activity of both the PNRC1 promoter and intron reporters was significantly enhanced in YAP/TAZ knockdown HCT116 cells.
source: In contrast, the luciferase activity of both the PNRC1 promoter and intron reporters was significantly enhanced in YAP/TAZ knockdown HCT116 cells (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation of the TEAD binding sites abolished the inhibitory effect of YAP5SA on the PNRC1 promoter and intron luciferase reporters.
source: Consistent with the above results, mutation of the TEAD binding sites abolished the inhibitory effect of YAP5SAon the PNRC1 promoter and intron luciferase reporters (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutation of the TEAD binding sites escaped the derepression of PNRC1 promoter and intron luciferase reporters by YAP/TAZ knockdown.
source: Similarly, mutation of the TEAD binding sites escaped the derepression of PNRC1 promoter and intron luciferase reporters by YAP/TAZ knockdown (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: YAP bound to the promoter and intronic regions of PNRC1, which required its interaction with TEADs.
source: Furthermore, the ChIP–qPCR results confirmed that YAP bound to the promoter and intronic regions of PNRC1, which required its interaction with TEADs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The NuRD complex component CHD4 was recruited to the promoter and intronic regions of the PNRC1 gene by overexpressed YAP5SA but not by the TEAD binding-defective YAP5SA-S94A mutant.
source: The ChIP–qPCR results showed that the NuRD complex component CHD4 was recruited to the promoter and intronic regions of the PNRC1 gene by overexpressed YAP5SA but not by the TEAD binding-defective YAP5SA-S94A mutant (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Knockdown of the NuRD complex components CHD4 and RBBP4 significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of PNRC1 in HCT116 cells.
source: Moreover, knockdown of the NuRD complex components CHD4 and RBBP4 significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of PNRC1 in HCT116 cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Knockdown of CHD4 significantly decreased the number of DDX6/DCP1A-positive foci in HCT116 cells.
source: Consistently, knockdown of CHD4 significantly decreased the number of DDX6/DCP1A-positive foci in HCT116 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: YAP/TAZ inhibits PNRC1 gene transcription through direct binding of TEADs to the PNRC1 gene locus and the NuRD complex is required for the transcriptional repression of PNRC1 by YAP/TAZ.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that YAP/TAZ inhibits PNRC1 gene transcription through direct binding of TEADs to the PNRC1 gene locus and that the NuRD complex is required for the transcriptional repression of PNRC1 by YAP/TAZ.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing TEAD binding, NuRD recruitment, and effects on PNRC1 expression.

claim: The mRNA level of PNRC1 was significantly decreased in colorectal cancer (CRC) according to analysis of TCGA datasets.
source: Analysis of colorectal (COAD) and rectal (READ) TCGA datasets revealed that the mRNA level of PNRC1 was significantly decreased in CRC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The mRNA level of PNRC1 was decreased in CRC tissues compared to paired normal mucosal tissues in 16 CRC patients.
source: We further confirmed the decreased mRNA level of PNRC1 in CRC by qPCR analysis of 16 CRC tissues with paired normal mucosal tissues; this finding implies that PNRC1 is a potential tumor suppressor also in CRC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from patient samples shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reexpression of WT PNRC1 almost completely abolished the increases in cell proliferation and colony formation induced by YAP5SA overexpression in HCT116 cells.
source: We observed that reexpression of WT PNRC1 almost completely abolished the increases in cell proliferation and colony formation induced by YAP5SA overexpression in HCT116 cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by CCK8 and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Re-expression of the PNRC1 W300A mutant did not affect the proliferation and colony formation of YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 cells.
source: Re-expression of the PNRC1 W300A mutant did not affect the proliferation and colony formation of YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 cells, which implied that the suppressive effect of PNRC1 on YAP relies on the recruitment of cytoplasmic DCP1A/DCP2 into the nucleolus by PNRC1 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by CCK8 and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5A and B, and inference about mechanism.

claim: Overexpression of PNRC1 WT but not PNRC1 W300A suppressed the increase in migration induced by YAP5SA in HCT116 cells.
source: Similarly, overexpression of PNRC1 WT but not PNRC1 W300A suppressed the increase in migration induced by YAP5SA in HCT116 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Reexpression of WT PNRC1 but not the W300A mutant dramatically inhibited the growth of YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 xenografts in nude mice.
source: Consistent with the above findings, reexpression of WT PNRC1 but not the W300A mutant dramatically inhibited the growth of YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 xenografts, and xenograft tumors formed from HCT116 cells coexpressing YAP5SA and PNRC1 were significantly smaller than the tumors formed from HCT116 cells expressing YAP5SA alone or in combination with the PNRC1 W300A mutant (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by xenograft tumor data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Xenograft tumors formed from HCT116 cells coexpressing YAP5SA and PNRC1 showed fewer Ki67-positive cells compared to tumors from cells expressing YAP5SA alone or with PNRC1 W300A.
source: Ki67 staining of xenograft tumors further showed fewer Ki67-positive cells in xenograft tumors formed from HCT116 cells coexpressing YAP5SA and PNRC1 (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The decrease in proliferation and attenuation of migration induced by YAP/TAZ knockdown were reversed by knockdown of PNRC1 in HCT116 cells.
source: Intriguingly, the decrease in proliferation and attenuation of migration induced by YAP/TAZ knockdown were reversed by knockdown of PNRC1 in HCT116 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by CCK8 and Transwell assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: YAP promotes tumorigenesis by downregulating PNRC1 expression and reexpression of PNRC1 suppresses YAP-driven tumor growth.
source: Overall, these results indicate that YAP promotes tumorigenesis by downregulating PNRC1 expression and that reexpression of PNRC1 suppresses YAP-driven tumor growth.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing effects of PNRC1 on YAP-induced oncogenic phenotypes.

claim: Knockdown of DCP1A, LSM14A, and DDX6 suppressed the proliferation of YAP5SA-expressing and control HCT116 cells.
source: Next, by using a CCK8 assay, we found that knockdown of DCP1A, LSM14A, and DDX6 suppressed the proliferation of YAP5SA-expressing and control 'parental' HCT116 cells, consistent with the results of the colony formation assay (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by CCK8 and colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Knockdown of DCP1A, LSM14A, and DDX6 led to downregulation of cell mitosis and increased cell apoptosis in HCT116 cells.
source: By analyzing the cell cycle and cell apoptosis, we further found that knockdown of DCP1A, LSM14A, and DDX6 all led to downregulation of cell mitosis and increased cell apoptosis, which was opposite to the effect of YAP5SA overexpression in HCT116 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle and apoptosis analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Knockdown of either DCP1A or LSM14A significantly attenuated the enhancement of cell migration induced by overexpression of YAP5SA in HCT116 cells.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of either DCP1A or LSM14A significantly attenuated the enhancement of cell migration induced by overexpression of YAP5SA in HCT116 cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by Transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of DDX6 showed stimulative effect on the migration of both control and YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 cells.
source: In contrast, knockdown of DDX6 showed stimulative effect on the migration of both control and YAP5SA-expressing HCT116 cells, possibly due to the diverse functions of DDX6 (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A; Di Stefano et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by Transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and citation to Di Stefano et al., 2019.

claim: Knockdown of AJUBA and SAMD4A suppressed the proliferation and cell migration of YAP5SA-expressing and control HCT116 cells.
source: Indeed, both knockdown of AJUBA and SAMD4A suppressed the proliferation and cell migration of YAP5SA-expressing and control 'parental' HCT116 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by CCK8 and Transwell assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4D and E.

claim: P-body formation is required for the oncogenic function of YAP in CRC.
source: Collectively, our data demonstrate that P-body formation is required for the oncogenic function of YAP in CRC.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing that disruption of P-bodies attenuates YAP-induced oncogenic phenotypes.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between YAP-regulated P-body-related genes (SAMD4A, AJUBA, and WTIP) and canonical target genes of YAP (CTGF, CYR61, AXL, and AMOTL2) in cell lines across cancers.
source: As expected, by analyzing gene expression data from the CCLE, we observed a strong positive correlation between YAP-regulated P-body-related genes (SAMD4A, AJUBA, and WTIP) and canonical target genes of YAP (CTGF, CYR61, AXL, and AMOTL2) in cell lines across cancers or in cell lines of colorectal, breast and lung lineages (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of CCLE data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The mRNA level of PNRC1 was negatively correlated with that of YAP target genes in cancer cells of thyroid and central nervous system (CNS) lineages.
source: Although there were no correlations between PNRC1 and YAP target genes in cell lines across cancers, we found that the mRNA level of PNRC1 was negatively correlated with that of YAP target genes in cancer cells of thyroid and central nervous system (CNS) lineages (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of CCLE data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IHC analysis of 294 CRC tissues showed positive correlation between the expression of AJUBA/SAMD4A and YAP.
source: IHC analysis of 294 CRC tissues further showed the positive correlation between the expression of AJUBA/SAMD4A and YAP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by IHC analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knockout of the P-body-nucleation-determining genes DDX6 and LSM14A inhibited proliferation in multiple cancer cell lines according to DepMap analysis.
source: Strikingly, knockout of the P-body-nucleation-determining genes DDX6 and LSM14A inhibited proliferation in multiple cancer cell lines (negative Chronos score) (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of DepMap CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Knockout of EDC4, which is required for P-body aggregation, inhibited proliferation in multiple cancer cell lines according to DepMap analysis.
source: Similar results were observed for EDC4, which is required for P-body aggregation (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of DepMap CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: YAP ranked 14th among genes correlating with EDC4 in DepMap dependency analysis.
source: Furthermore, we found that YAP ranked 14th among genes correlating with EDC4 (Figure 7C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of DepMap data shown in Figure 7C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The YAP dependency score was positively correlated with the DDX6 and LSM14A scores in DepMap analysis.
source: In addition, the YAP dependency score was positively correlated with the DDX6 and LSM14A scores (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of DepMap data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The knockdown of DCP1A/LSM14A and overexpression of PNRC1 attenuated both cell proliferation and cell migration in MCF7, MDA-MB-231, and A549 cell lines.
source: Consistent with the observation in HCT116 cells, the knockdown of DCP1A/LSM14A and overexpression of PNRC1 attenuated both cell proliferation and cell migration in these three YAP-dependent cancer cells (Figure 7—figure supplements 3–5).
evidence: Supported by CCK8 and Transwell assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: The co-dependencies of YAP/TEAD and essential P-body genes suggest that enhanced P-body formation plays a vital role in YAP-induced tumorigenesis.
source: Collectively, the co-dependencies of YAP/TEAD and essential P-body genes further suggest that enhanced P-body formation plays a vital role in YAP-induced tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inferred from DepMap analysis showing correlations between YAP/TEAD and P-body gene dependencies.

claim: YAP was reported to be a negative regulator of P-bodies and to be involved in Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KHSV)-induced P-body disassembly in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs).
source: Recently, YAP was reported to be a negative regulator of P-bodies and to be involved in Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KHSV)-induced P-body disassembly in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) (Castle et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castle et al., 2021.

claim: The formation of P-bodies is correlated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in breast cancer.
source: The formation of P-bodies is correlated with epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in breast cancer (Hardy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hardy et al., 2017.

claim: There is evidence that an increase in P-bodies leads to attenuated growth, migration, and invasion of prostate cancer cells.
source: In contrast, there is also evidence that an increase in P-bodies leads to attenuated growth, migration, and invasion of prostate cancer cells (Bearss et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bearss et al., 2021.

claim: P-bodies are cytoplasmic membraneless organelles that consist of ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) and are formed by phase separation.
source: Processing bodies (P-bodies) are cytoplasmic membraneless organelles that consist of ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) and are formed by phase separation (Luo et al., 2018; Riggs et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 2018 and Riggs et al., 2020.

claim: The primary function of P-bodies is controlling the storage of untranslated mRNAs.
source: Although initial studies hypothesized that mRNAs in P-bodies are targeted for decay and translational repression, it was subsequently suggested that P-bodies are not required for mRNA decay and that repressed mRNAs can be recycled from P-bodies to reenter translation; thus, the primary function of P-bodies is controlling the storage of untranslated mRNAs (Decker and Parker, 2012; Hubstenberger et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Decker and Parker, 2012; Hubstenberger et al., 2017; and Luo et al., 2018.

claim: YAP/TAZ can function as corepressors to inhibit target gene transcription by recruiting the nucleosome remodeling and histone deacetylase (NuRD) complex.
source: Although initially identified as transcriptional coactivators, YAP/TAZ can also function as corepressors to inhibit target gene transcription by recruiting the nucleosome remodeling and histone deacetylase (NuRD) complex (Kim et al., 2015b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015b.

claim: The Hippo pathway is an evolutionally conserved signaling pathway that regulates organ size and plays vital roles in development and tissue homeostasis.
source: The Hippo pathway is an evolutionally conserved signaling pathway that regulates organ size and plays vital roles in development and tissue homeostasis (Driskill and Pan, 2021; Ma et al., 2019; Russell and Camargo, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Driskill and Pan, 2021; Ma et al., 2019; and Russell and Camargo, 2022.

claim: Dysregulation of YAP/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional output endows tumor cells with every hallmark of cancer, including sustained proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, tumor-promoting inflammation, tumor immune escape, and dysregulated tumor metabolism.
source: Dysregulation of YAP/TAZ-TEAD transcriptional output endows tumor cells with every hallmark of cancer, including sustained proliferation, resistance to apoptosis, tumor-promoting inflammation, tumor immune escape, dysregulated tumor metabolism, etc. (Calses et al., 2019; Hanahan, 2022; Kulkarni et al., 2020; Nguyen and Yi, 2019; Zanconato et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Calses et al., 2019; Hanahan, 2022; Kulkarni et al., 2020; Nguyen and Yi, 2019; and Zanconato et al., 2016.

claim: PNRC1 translocates the cytoplasmic DCP1A/DCP2 decapping complex into the nucleolus, which subsequently impedes rRNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis.
source: PNRC1 translocates the cytoplasmic DCP1A/DCP2 decapping complex into the nucleolus, which subsequently impedes rRNA transcription and ribosome biogenesis (Gaviraghi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaviraghi et al., 2018.

claim: Hemizygous deletion of the 6q15 locus, where PNRC1 is located, occurs in multiple cancers, including prostate, pancreatic, breast, and liver cancers.
source: Moreover, hemizygous deletion of the 6q15 locus, where PNRC1 is located, occurs in multiple cancers, including prostate, pancreatic, breast, and liver cancers (Gaviraghi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaviraghi et al., 2018.

claim: PNRC1 inhibits RAS- and MYC-driven tumor cell proliferation.
source: It has been shown that PNRC1 inhibits RAS- and MYC-driven tumor cell proliferation (Gaviraghi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaviraghi et al., 2018.

claim: YAP acts downstream of mutant KRAS, and activation of YAP was found to drive KRAS-independent tumor relapse in preclinical models of pancreatic cancer.
source: In addition, YAP acts downstream of mutant KRAS, and activation of YAP was found to drive KRAS-independent tumor relapse in preclinical models of pancreatic cancer (Kapoor et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kapoor et al., 2014; Shao et al., 2014; and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Reexpression of PNRC1 or disruption of P-bodies is a potential therapeutic strategy for tumors with active YAP.
source: Our study suggests that the P-body is a new downstream effector of YAP/TAZ, which implies that reexpression of PNRC1 or disruption of P-bodies is a potential therapeutic strategy for tumors with active YAP.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing that PNRC1 reexpression and P-body disruption attenuate YAP-induced oncogenic phenotypes.

claim: Transcriptional downregulation of PNRC1 by YAP activation could be a new mechanism of PNRC1 dysregulation during tumorigenesis.
source: Our findings suggest that transcriptional downregulation of PNRC1 by YAP activation could be a new mechanism of PNRC1 dysregulation during tumorigenesis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing YAP-mediated transcriptional repression of PNRC1.

claim: The presence of the YAP-PNRC1 regulatory axis implies a potential role of YAP in ribosome biogenesis.
source: The presence of the YAP-PNRC1 regulatory axis implies a potential role of YAP in ribosome biogenesis, which warrants further investigation in follow-up studies.
evidence: Inferred from the known role of PNRC1 in ribosome biogenesis and the YAP-PNRC1 regulatory relationship.

claim: The identification of the P-body as a new downstream effector of YAP/TAZ suggests that disruption of P-bodies might be a potential therapeutic strategy for tumors with active YAP.
source: The identification of the P-body as a new downstream effector of YAP/TAZ suggests that disruption of P-bodies might be a potential therapeutic strategy for tumors with active YAP.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and DepMap analysis showing importance of P-bodies for YAP-dependent cell proliferation.

claim: YAP/TAZ promote P-body formation in a series of cancer cell lines.
source: Here, we showed that the oncogenes YAP/TAZ promote P-body formation in a series of cancer cell lines.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased P-bodies upon YAP/TAZ activation in multiple cell lines.

claim: Both transcriptional activation of the P-body-related genes SAMD4A, AJUBA, and WTIP and transcriptional suppression of the tumor suppressor gene PNRC1 are involved in enhancing the effects of YAP/TAZ on P-body formation in colorectal cancer (CRC) cells.
source: Mechanistically, both transcriptional activation of the P-body-related genes SAMD4A, AJUBA, and WTIP and transcriptional suppression of the tumor suppressor gene PNRC1 are involved in enhancing the effects of YAP/TAZ on P-body formation in colorectal cancer (CRC) cells.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data and functional experiments showing these genes mediate YAP/TAZ effects on P-bodies.

claim: Disruption of P-bodies attenuates cell proliferation, cell migration, and tumor growth induced by overexpression of YAP5SA in CRC.
source: By reexpression of PNRC1 or knockdown of P-body core genes (DDX6, DCP1A, and LSM14A), we determined that disruption of P-bodies attenuates cell proliferation, cell migration, and tumor growth induced by overexpression of YAP5SA in CRC.
evidence: Supported by proliferation, migration, and xenograft assay data.

evidence: Supported by analysis of DepMap CRISPR screen data.

claim: The role of P-bodies in tumorigenesis and tumor progression is not well understood.
source: The role of processing bodies (P-bodies) in tumorigenesis and tumor progression is not well understood.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about the limited understanding of P-bodies in cancer.

claim: DDX6 and DCP1A are essential components of P-bodies and are normally used as biomarkers for P-bodies.
source: DEAD-box ATP-dependent RNA helicase 6 (DDX6) and mRNA-decapping enzyme 1A (DCP1A) are the essential components of P-bodies and are normally used as the biomarkers for P-bodies (James et al., 2010; Lavalée et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to James et al., 2010; Lavalée et al., 2021; and Luo et al., 2018.

claim: P-body formation is constitutive and independent of the activation of the integrated stress response (ISR).
source: In contrast to stress granule (SG) formation, P-body formation is constitutive and independent of the activation of the integrated stress response (ISR) (Luo et al., 2018; Riggs et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 2018 and Riggs et al., 2020.

claim: The size and number of P-bodies are altered in response to stress.
source: Moreover, despite their constitutive formation in cells, the size and number of P-bodies are altered in response to stress (Luo et al., 2018; Riggs et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Luo et al., 2018 and Riggs et al., 2020.

claim: The proteins LSM14A and DDX6 are essential nucleating proteins for P-body assembly.

evidence: Supported by citations to Lavalée et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2018; and Riggs et al., 2020.

claim: TGF-β induces P-body formation and EMT in mammary epithelial cells.

evidence: Supported by citation to Hardy et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of P-body formation by knockdown of DDX6 reverses EMT and suppresses breast cancer metastasis.
